title.text:
Data as tables: records,
variables and keys

objects.text: What exactly is one row of a table, and how does one table connect to another?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 2 of 24  |  Module A: Think with data
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session we drew the map of the whole course. Today we look closely at the thing every later session depends on, the table. You will open the Lakeside Mart workbook and learn to read a table the way a data scientist does: what one row stands for, how a column is measured, and how one table links to another.

These ideas decide whether a total you report is right or wrong, so we take our time.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can say what one record of a table stands for, which is its granularity, and you can pick the right variable type for every variable. You can find a primary key, a composite key and a foreign key, and read a diagram that shows how tables link.

And you can test a table in Google Sheets for missing values and messy data, and then write a data dictionary. You will do all of it on the Lakeside Mart workbook, with no code.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts
first, then a Google Sheets lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_c6bc7973.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the sheet. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 1 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with no laptops open, so you can watch the pictures. After a ten minute break we open the Lakeside Mart workbook in Google Sheets for a forty-five minute lab.

You will predict each answer, check it with a formula, and write what you find on a new tab. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  In CRISP-DM, which phase comes straight after business understanding, and what do you do in it?
2.  In Excel words, what is a dataset, and how does a model differ from a formula?
3.  An assistant gives you the share of orders paid by Mobile money. What do you do before you report it?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 1. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. In CRISP-DM, which phase comes straight after business understanding, and what do you do in it?

A good answer is this. Data understanding: find the tables that could answer the question and check what they mean.

Question two. In Excel words, what is a dataset, and how does a model differ from a formula?

A good answer is this. A dataset is a workbook in which each tab is one table. A model is a rule found from data, where a formula is typed by a person.

Question three. An assistant gives you the share of orders paid by Mobile money. What do you do before you report it?

A good answer is this. Recompute it from your own data: 48.8 percent, 976 of 2,000. Write the source beside it.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. After business understanding, the next CRISP-DM phase is data understanding. You cannot answer a question until you know which tables could answer it and what they mean, and that is exactly where we are today. title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: One row of a table: one thing the table describes. In the orders tab each record is one till order.
The level of detail of a table: one record per order, per order line or per branch per week.
Variable type: how a variable is measured (numeric, categorical, datetime, text). Data type: how the cell stores it (integer, float, string). They are different ideas.
A primary key never repeats and names one record. A foreign key holds the primary key of another table and links the two.
A cell with no value. Ask whether it means unknown, not applicable or something real. Informative missingness: the blank itself is a fact, such as a walk-in shopper.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_notebook_0.66.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_key_0.66.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Record (observation, instance, row). One row of a table: one thing the table describes. In the orders tab each record is one till order.

Granularity (grain). The level of detail of a table: one record per order, per order line or per branch per week.

Variable type and data type. Variable type: how a variable is measured (numeric, categorical, datetime, text). Data type: how the cell stores it (integer, float, string). They are different ideas.

Primary key and foreign key. A primary key never repeats and names one record. A foreign key holds the primary key of another table and links the two.

Missing value (NaN, NULL). A cell with no value. Ask whether it means unknown, not applicable or something real. Informative missingness: the blank itself is a fact, such as a walk-in shopper.

title.text:
A table holds records in rows
and variables in columns

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_anatomy_7.70x4.80_5844d5a2.png
objects.alt: A table holds records in rows and variables in columns

objects.text: A record is one row. A variable is one column.

runs.text: Record (observation, instance): one row. Here, one till order.
Variable (feature, field): one column.
Cell: one value of one variable in one record.

slides.notes:
Here are the first four rows of the orders tab of the Lakeside Mart workbook. The whole grid is one table. Each column is a variable, which is one fact recorded for every order, such as the order date. Each row is a record. Data scientists also call it an observation or an instance, and in machine learning you will hear instance.

In this table each record is one till order. And a cell is a single value, one variable for one record. Look at the gold cell: it holds the customer id of the fourth order. Notice two empty cells in the customer column. We come back to them.

Can you point to one record on the slide?

title.text:
The spreadsheet word and the
data science word for each part

rows.text: One thing the table describes, such as one till order.
The same fact about every record, such as branch_id.
All the records of one kind.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_grid_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_pin_0.38.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_doc_0.38.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_folder_0.38.png

objects.text: In machine learning a variable is either a feature (an input) or the target (the answer you predict).

slides.notes:
You already know every part of a table from Excel, so here is the translation. A row is a record, also called an observation or an instance. A column is a variable, also called a feature, a field or an attribute. A cell holds a value. A tab is a table, and in pandas, the Python library we meet in Session 7, a table is called a DataFrame.

A whole workbook is a dataset, or a database when it is stored in a system. The words differ between statistics, databases and machine learning, but the idea is the same. When you read documentation or a job advert, this table is your dictionary. Which of these words was new to you?

title.text:
Granularity is the level of detail: one record per
order, per order line or per branch per week

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_granularity_7.70x4.80_70d3c723.png
objects.alt: Granularity is the level of detail: one record per order, per order line or per branch per week

objects.text: Granularity is the level of detail of a table. It says what one record stands for.

runs.text: The unit of observation is what one record stands for.
Data warehouse teams call the level of detail the grain.
Finish this sentence first: each record is one ...

slides.notes:
Now the question in the title of today: what exactly is one row?

The standard name is granularity, the level of detail of a table. What one record stands for is called the unit of observation. People who build data warehouses call this the grain, so if a colleague says grain, they mean the same thing. Look at the picture. The same order, O000003, appears at three levels.

In orders it is one record. In order_lines it is two records, one for each product. And branch_weeks has one record for a whole branch and a whole week. Before you count or total anything, finish the sentence: each record is one what?

title.text:
Each of the six tabs has its
own record and its own count

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_shop_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_person_0.39.png

objects.text: The workbook holds a 2,000-order sample of the full Lakeside Mart file. Records are counted without the header row.

slides.notes:
Here are the six data tabs of your workbook, each with its unit of observation. Orders has 2,000 records, one per till order. Order lines has 6,590, one per product on an order. Products has 150, branches has 8, customers has 2,500 loyalty customers, and branch weeks has 832, one for each branch in each week.

There is also a seventh tab called READ ME, which is only a note. The workbook holds a sample of two thousand orders from the full file, so totals here will differ from the full file. Session 4 explains why. In the lab you will write this table yourself on a new tab.

title.text:
Counting records in the wrong tab:
6,590 lines are not 6,590 orders

objects.text: Wrong

runs.text: order_lines has 6,590 records.
Reporting that as the number of orders counts every product on every order.

objects.text: Right

runs.text: Count the orders tab: 2,000 orders.
Or count each order_id once in order_lines: 2,000.
That is 3.3 lines per order on average.

objects.text: State the granularity first. Then count.

slides.notes:
This is the most common mistake with tables. You open the order lines tab, you see 6,590 rows, and you tell your manager the shop sold 6,590 orders. Nothing warns you. But a record in order lines is one product on one order, and a basket of five products adds five records.

The orders tab has 2,000 orders, and the lines average 3.3 per order, which is 6,590 divided by 2,000. To count each order once in the order lines, use COUNTA of UNIQUE of the order id range. So say the granularity first, then count. Which tab would you count to get the number of customers who bought something?

title.text:
Every variable has a variable type (how it is
measured) and a data type (how it is stored)

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_types_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Every variable has a variable type (how it is measured) and a data type (how it is stored)

objects.text: Discrete: counted. Continuous: measured. An identifier (order_id) is a label: never add it up.

slides.notes:
Every variable has two kinds of type, and people mix them up. The variable type is how the value is measured. Numeric values are numbers you can add. They are discrete when you count them, like quantity, and continuous when you measure them, like money. Categorical values are labels.

They are nominal when there is no order, like payment method, and ordinal when there is an order, like Basic, Silver and Gold. Datetime values are dates and times, and text is free words. The data type is how the cell stores it: integer, float, string or datetime.

A date can be stored as a string, and we will see that happen in this workbook. An identifier such as order_id or customer_id names a record, so you never add it up. Which type is branch_id?

title.text:
The seven variables of the
orders tab and their types

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_key_0.33.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_shop_0.33.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_person_0.33.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_coin_0.33.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.33.png

objects.text: An identifier can look like a number or a code. You never add it up.

slides.notes:
Now we apply both kinds of type to the seven variables of the orders tab. Order_id and customer_id are identifiers, labels that name something, and you never average a label. Order_date should be a datetime, but in this workbook it is stored as a string, which is text.

We test that in the lab with a function called ISNUMBER. Branch_id and payment_method are categorical with no order. Promo_week is stored as an integer, but it only holds zero or one, so it is a categorical flag. And order_value_ugx is numeric, a continuous amount in shillings. Why does the type matter?

Because it decides which questions make sense. Would an average of branch_id mean anything?

title.text:
A primary key is a variable that
is different in every record

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_key_test_7.70x4.80_7a8658fa.png
objects.alt: A primary key is a variable that is different in every record

objects.text: Primary key: a variable whose value is different in every record, so it names exactly one record.

runs.text: Test it: count the filled cells, then count the different values.
If the two counts match, it can be a primary key.
order_id passes. customer_id repeats, so it fails.

slides.notes:
A primary key is a variable whose value never repeats, so it names exactly one record, like an invoice number in Excel. You can test a candidate in two steps. First count the filled cells with COUNTA. Then count the different values with COUNTA of UNIQUE, a Google Sheets formula.

For order_id both counts are 2,000, so order_id is the primary key of the orders tab. For customer_id the first count is 1,420 and the second is only 1,082. Some customers ordered more than once, so the value repeats. Customer_id is not a key of the orders tab.

With blanks in a range, use COUNTUNIQUE in Sheets. Which variable would you test as the key of the order lines tab?

title.text: Two variables together can form a composite key

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_composite_7.70x4.80_fae88759.png
objects.alt: Two variables together can form a composite key

objects.text: Composite key: two or more variables that are unique together, although each repeats alone.

runs.text: branch_id repeats: every branch appears once per week.
week_start repeats: every week appears once per branch.
Each pair appears once, so the pair is the key: 832 records.

slides.notes:
Sometimes no single variable is unique. Look at the branch weeks tab. Branch_id repeats, because every branch appears in every week. Week_start repeats too, because every week appears for every branch. But the pair, branch and week together, never repeats. That is a composite key. There are 8 branches and 104 weeks, and 8 times 104 is 832, which is exactly the number of records in the tab.

The product matches the record count, which fits with every pair appearing once but does not prove it. The proof is to count the distinct pairs and get the same number again, which you do in the lab. Where else might you meet a pair like this at work?

title.text:
A foreign key holds the primary key
of another table and links the two

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_fk_7.70x4.80_7192d620.png
objects.alt: A foreign key holds the primary key of another table and links the two

objects.text: Foreign key: a variable whose values are primary keys of another table.

runs.text: branch_id in orders is a foreign key. branch_id in branches is the primary key.
Look up B01 in branches to find the branch name.
In SQL and pandas this lookup is called a join or a merge.

slides.notes:
A foreign key is a variable in one table that holds the primary key of another table. Look at the picture. The orders tab on the left has a branch_id on every order. That branch_id is a foreign key. The branches tab on the right has one record per branch, and there branch_id is the primary key.

Each arrow goes from an order to the one branch record it belongs to. You already do this lookup in Excel with VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP, where B01 returns Kampala Central. In SQL and in pandas the same step is called a join or a merge, and we meet it in later sessions.

Which other variable in orders is a foreign key?

title.text:
Tables relate one-to-many: one branch has
many orders and one order has many lines

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_onemany_7.70x4.80_e0dd01bf.png
objects.alt: Tables relate one-to-many: one branch has many orders and one order has many lines

objects.text: A relationship says how records of two tables match. The common kind is one-to-many.

runs.text: One branch has many orders: B01 has 372.
One order has many lines: O000003 has 2.
Many-to-many: orders and products, joined by the junction table order_lines.

slides.notes:
A relationship says how the records of two tables match. The most common kind is one-to-many. One branch has many orders: in this sample branch B01 has 372. One order has many lines: order O000003 has 2, and the largest basket in the sample has 19. Read from the other side it is many-to-one: many orders belong to one branch.

The lines on the picture end in three prongs on the many side. There is a third kind, many-to-many. Products and orders are like that, because a product appears on many orders and an order has many products. The order lines tab sits in between as a junction table, also called a bridge table, and turns it into two one-to-many links.

Is customers to orders one-to-many?

title.text:
An entity relationship diagram (ERD)
draws the six tabs and how their keys link

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_erd_11.90x4.25_498dd7cb.png
objects.alt: An entity relationship diagram (ERD) draws the six tabs and how their keys link

objects.text: PK marks a primary key and FK a foreign key. A line ends in three prongs on its many side.

slides.notes:
This picture is an entity relationship diagram, or ERD. It is the standard way to draw how tables link. Each box is a table, with its primary key marked PK and its foreign keys marked FK. Each line is a one-to-many relationship, and the three prongs sit on the many side.

Orders points to customers and to branches. Order lines points to orders and to products. Branch weeks points to branches, and its branch id is part of a composite key. Customers also holds a home branch id that points to branches, which is the line that goes over the top.

Each box shows only some of its variables. Which table would you start from to find the branch of a product sold?

title.text:
Follow order O000003
through four tabs by their keys

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_trace_11.90x4.25_5a6d630a.png
objects.alt: Follow order O000003 through four tabs by their keys

objects.text: customer_id is blank, so this order has no row in customers: it was a walk-in.

slides.notes:
Let us follow one order through the tabs using only keys. Start in the orders tab: order O000003, at branch B01, with a value of 66,200 shillings. Step one, look up its order_id in the order lines tab. You find 2 lines, for products P117 and P043. Step two, look those product ids up in the products tab to get their names.

Step three, look the branch id up in branches: Kampala Central. The two line amounts, 58,400 and 7,800, add up to 66,200, the order total. The customer id is blank, so there is no customer to look up. Why do you think that is?

title.text:
A blank customer_id is a missing value,
and it appears on 29 percent of orders

objects.text: 580 of the 2,000 orders have no customer_id. The data dictionary says the blank means a walk-in: a shopper with no loyalty number.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_e55a5fee.png
objects.alt: A blank customer_id is a missing value, and it appears on 29 percent of orders

slides.notes:
Now missing values. A missing value is a cell with no value. In the orders tab, 580 of the 2,000 orders have a blank customer id, which is 29 percent, about 29 orders in every 100. Before you delete those rows or fill them in, ask what the blank means.

The data dictionary tells us: the shopper was a walk-in, with no loyalty number. So the blank is not an error. It records a real fact about the shopper. We call that informative missingness. If you deleted these records you would throw away three out of ten orders.

What would you do with them if you wanted the average spend of loyalty customers only?

title.text:
A blank can mean unknown, not applicable or
a walk-in, and each needs different handling

rows.text: Unknown: the value exists but was not recorded
loans.csv: 379 of 8,000 loans have no monthly_income_ugx
Impute (fill in) with the median, and add a missing-indicator flag
Not applicable: no value can exist
Illustrative: a refund reason on an order that was never refunded
Leave it blank, or write none
Informative missingness: the blank itself is a fact
orders: 580 blank customer_id values mean a walk-in
Keep it, and add a flag such as is_walk_in

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_person_0.50.png

objects.text: Names for a blank: NaN in pandas, NULL in SQL, an empty cell in Sheets.

slides.notes:
Not every blank means the same thing, and each meaning needs different handling. A blank can mean unknown: the value exists but nobody recorded it, like the 379 loans out of 8,000 in the Nile Microfinance file with no monthly income. There, a common fix is imputation, which means filling in the blank with the median, and adding a flag column so you remember which values were filled.

A blank can mean not applicable, like a refund reason on an order that was never refunded. That example is made up. Or the blank can be informative, like our walk-in customers. There you keep the blank and add a flag. Tools name it differently: NaN in pandas, NULL in SQL.

Which of the three is a blank in your own data?

slides.notes:
Real exports are messy. This is a small piece of a raw order line export, the file we clean in Session 8. The gold cells are the problems. One date is written day, month, year while most are year, month, day. A branch name is misspelt. Mobile money appears as MM.

One quantity is missing, and one price is stored as text with the letters UGX in front. Across the whole file the three payment methods appear under 11 different spellings, and the eight branches under 26. A pivot table would treat each spelling as a separate group and quietly give you wrong totals.

Which of these would be hardest to spot in a file of forty thousand rows?

Here are six checks you can run on any table before you trust a total, each with the Sheets formula and a real finding. Blank cells: COUNTBLANK found 580 in customer id. Dates stored as text: ISNUMBER on an order date returns FALSE. Inconsistent labels: the raw export has 11 spellings of three payment methods, which COUNTUNIQUE reveals in Sheets.

In Excel 365 use COUNTA of UNIQUE of FILTER. Extreme values: the largest order is 1,935,520 shillings against a median of 24,800. Duplicates: the raw export has 80 exact duplicate lines. And numbers stored as text, like UGX 1,700. In the lab you will run the first, second and fourth of these.

Which check would you run first on a file someone emails you?

The last idea is the data dictionary. It is a short document that explains every variable in a table: its meaning, its variable type and its key. Look at the orders tab written as a dictionary. The gold cell is the one that saves you from a wrong decision.

It says that customer id is blank for a walk-in, so you do not delete or fill those records. Without that line, someone would call the blanks an error. The full Lakeside dictionary comes with your workbook files. A good dictionary lets a new colleague read the table without asking you anything.

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1 counts the filled cells of order_id: 2,000 records.
Line 2 counts the different values. Equal to line 1 means a primary key.
Line 3 counts the empty cells of customer_id: 580.
Line 4 counts the orders paid by Mobile money: 976.
Line 5 is TRUE for a real date or number. Here it is FALSE: the date is text.

slides.notes:
Before the lab, read the five formulas that do most of the work. Line one, COUNTA of A2 to A2001, counts the filled cells in the order id column, which gives 2,000. Line two counts the different values: if it equals line one, the variable can be a primary key.

Line three, COUNTBLANK on the customer column, counts the empty cells and gives 580. Line four, COUNTIF, counts the records where the payment method is Mobile money, 976. Line five, ISNUMBER on B2, says whether the date is a real date, and here it says FALSE. Tab names go in front of the range with an exclamation mark, like orders!A2:A2001, when you work from another tab.

Which formula would you use to count orders paid by cash?

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: A count of 2,001 where you expected 2,000
The range includes the header cell in row 1.
Start the range in row 2: A2:A2001.
#REF! or #NAME? when you point to another tab
The tab name is missing or misspelt.
Write the tab, then !, then the range: orders!A2:A2001.
The key was not found, or FALSE is missing.
Add FALSE as the last argument. Check for stray spaces.
Cells below the UNIQUE formula hold data.
Clear them, or move the formula to an empty column.
ISNUMBER on a date gives FALSE
That is correct: the date is stored as text.
Write it on your dictionary tab as a finding.

slides.notes:
Five messages you may meet. A count that is one too big means your range includes the header row, so start in row 2. Hash REF or hash NAME when you point to another tab means the tab name is missing or misspelt, so write the tab, an exclamation mark and then the range.

Hash N A from VLOOKUP means the key was not found, or you forgot FALSE as the last argument. The message array result was not expanded means the cells below a UNIQUE formula already hold data, so clear them. And ISNUMBER returning FALSE on a date is correct, because the date is stored as text.

That one is a finding, so write it down. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.
